public_rationale: The announcement disclosed that humans used the model to prepare its arguments into manuscripts. Contemporaneous reporting confirms that this was part of the release. That is information about how the results were produced, and human involvement is expressly among Marcus's questions. It contradicts the categorical no-information assertion. It does not establish that the methodological disclosure was adequate or reproducible.
limitations: The verdict concerns no information, not the stronger question of adequate scientific disclosure.
Marketing, not science is left unscored.
Timing is supported by contemporaneous reporting rather than a complete archived launch snapshot.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI's Astra announcement was marketing rather than science and disclosed no information about how the results were achieved.

statement.excerpt: Yesterday's tweet and blog were marketing, not science. Neither of those nor the 249-page math article that went with them give any information about how this was accomplished:
statement.document_title: OpenAI’s amazing — but vastly oversold — new model Astra

from_speaker: give any information about how this was accomplished
our_interpretation: I assess the factual assertion that the named materials disclosed no information about the process.
The surrounding examples make human involvement and proof verification relevant process information.
Some substantive process information contradicts no information; it need not provide a reproducible account of model training or operation.
Marketing, not science is an evaluative characterization and receives no separate factual verdict.
criteria.support_condition: The launch versions of the named tweet, blog, and article contain no substantive information about model operation, human involvement, proof verification, or the process used to obtain the results.
criteria.contradiction_condition: At least one named launch document discloses substantive information about one of those aspects of the process.
